transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-15
Start time: 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Morgan Lee (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jade Nguyen (Redwood CSM), Elena Rossi (Auriga CISO), Tom Baxter (Auriga Head of Platform), Priya Singh (Auriga Compliance), Markus Lee (Auriga Ops)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
Auriga is evaluating BYOK/BYOK escrow options for Redwood-hosted inference and Private deployment. Key discussion points: envelope keys, HSM integration, rotation cadence, escrow/zeroization, audit log granularity, and SOC2 evidence. Action items: Redwood to share HSM playbook and run pilot; customer to provide KMS policy matrix.

Topics covered:
- Encryption at rest and in transit; envelope encryption flow
- BYOK flows: customer-hosted KMS vs Redwood-hosted wrap keys
- HSM onboarding options and split-key/escrow considerations
- Key rotation frequency, rollback and zeroization process
- Audit logs: key usage, request ids, retention and export for compliance
- Deployment modes (Hosted vs Private) and network/trust boundaries

Transcript (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect):
[00:00:03] Morgan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — we'll go 60-ish minutes. Samir's gonna run through the technical flow and then we'll talk ops.
[00:00:22] Elena (CISO): Thanks. We're mainly focused on how Redwood will access keys for hosted inference and what controls we get around rotation and escrow. Also need clarity for our SOC 2 auditor on log retention.
[00:00:35] Samir (SE): Right, high level — Redwood supports envelope encryption. Customer master keys (CMK) live in your KMS or in an HSM; we never see the plaintext root. For hosted customers we support two modes: 1) customer BYOK where we perform a key-wrapping handshake and never persist plaintext, 2) customer-managed HSM in Private where the call chain goes to your HSM in VPC.
[00:01:05] Tom (Head of Platform): Quick question — when you say "wrap", do you mean you store a wrapped key blob on Redwood side and unwrap at time of use? That is, does Redwood ever have a long-lived unwrapped key in memory?
[00:01:22] Samir (SE): Good callout. We store only a wrapped key blob. At runtime we unwrap ephemeral data keys inside a secure enclave on the inference host, scoped to the process and zeroized after use. There's also an optional HSM-delegation path where crypto operations are proxied to the customer's HSM so no unwrapping occurs in Redwood.
[00:01:55] Elena: That proxy path is interesting. Our policy says root keys must never leave our HSM, and ideally any unwrapped key material can't live outside a certified boundary. Which HSM vendors or standards do you support?
[00:02:12] Samir: We support PKCS#11 compatible modules — we've tested with Thales and AWS CloudHSM in our Private offering. For hosted BYOK we support wrapping/unwrapping via a customer-provided KMS endpoint (KMS REST gRPC) with mutual TLS — although there's a small performance tradeoff because of network round-trip.
[00:02:40] Markus (Ops): What's the typical P95 latency hit if we do on-demand unwrap for each inference call? We're very latency sensitive.
[00:02:49] Samir: If you unwrap per request that's expensive — seconds-range — so the common pattern is to unwrap a data key and cache it in memory for a bounded TTL, e.g., 15 minutes, and use envelope encryption to encrypt tokens and KV cache. We also do TTL-bounded ephemeral key caches tied to process lifetime, and we post metrics to the console so you can monitor cache miss rates. For strict customers we can use an HSM proxy in the same VPC which keeps latency low.
[00:03:22] Priya (Compliance): That in-memory cache thing — auditors will ask how it's protected. Do you provide attestations around the enclave or memory zeroization?
[00:03:29] Samir: We provide technical design docs and can supply enclave attestation artifacts for Private deployments; for hosted we have hardened processes and can provide SOC 2 Type II report and a redacted architecture review. But, yes, we need to provide memory zeroization procedure details for auditors.
[00:03:50] Elena: Also curious about rotation: our policy mandates rotation every 90 days for data keys and yearly for root keys. How does Redwood handle rotation and re-encryption of persisted artifacts?
[00:04:04] Samir: We have a rolling rotation process. For data keys we issue new data keys and rewrap relevant blobs in the background; we support online rewrap so you don't need downtime. Root key rotation is supported via key versioning in the wrapped blob format. Re-encryption is done lazily for cold objects and proactively for hot caches. We'll show the sequence diagram in the playbook.
[00:04:29] Tom: If you rotate a root key and something fails during rewrap, what's the rollback story? Can we rollback to previous keys gracefully?
[00:04:36] Samir: Yes — every wrap includes key version metadata. Our orchestration can roll back to the prior key version until you confirm data consistency. We also keep an audit trail of rewrap operations with request ids.
[00:04:52] Elena: About escrow — there's pushback internally about escrow purporting to be "extra safety" but being a liability. We want to understand options: full escrow to a third-party, split-escrow, or no escrow with enforced multi-person approval.
[00:05:06] Morgan (AE): To be clear, escrow is optional. We can do a split-key where parts of a root key are held by different parties, or you can keep keys fully in your HSM and Redwood never holds any escrow. There's also an archival escrow model where encrypted key shares are stored in a custody service that requires multi-sig to recover.
[00:05:26] Priya: Is split-key supported in the hosted flow?
[00:05:29] Samir: Split-key is tricky for multi-tenant hosted. For hosted we recommend customer-provided KMS endpoint or a wrapped-key with a short TTL and strong auditing. Split-key and multi-sig custody typically happen in Private/on-prem because it requires network and operational control.
[00:05:46] Markus: On audit logs — what do they include? We need per-request key usage, who requested it, token id, and a mapping to the call in Redwood so auditors can tie it back to sessions.
[00:05:56] Samir: Our audit logs capture key id, key version, operation (unwrap/wrap/sign), timestamp, request id, and the Redwood tenancy id. For hosted we redact user PII but include token hashes. We can push logs to your SIEM via secure streaming (TLS) or S3 export with encryption. Retention is configurable; default 90 days, can be extended for enterprise.
[00:06:21] Tom: If logs are exported to our SIEM, is there a guaranteed ordering / integrity? Auditors ask about tamper evidence.
[00:06:29] Samir: We support signed log bundles (HMAC with a rotation-protected key) for tamper evidence and immutable write-once buckets if needed. For Private we can integrate with your WORM storage.
[00:06:43] Elena: Can we get a sample of the log schema for auditors?
[00:06:46] Morgan: We'll include a schema excerpt in the playbook.
[00:06:49] Jade (CSM): Also to note — on SOC 2, we have a standard SOC 2 package plus attestations for our hosting. For Private customers we can include additional documentation.
[00:07:00] Elena: Great. Two more specific things: 1) key zeroization policies on deprovision, and 2) cross-region key access for DR.
[00:07:08] Samir: Zeroization — when a tenant is deprovisioned, we remove wrapped blobs and rotate the wrapping key so previous blobs are unrecoverable, plus we instruct any cached ephemeral keys to be zeroized; for Private we can do HSM zeroize commands. For cross-region DR we replicate wrapped blobs, but root keys stay in the customer KMS or HSM; replication includes metadata about versioning.
[00:07:34] Priya: For regulators we need proof that in case of subpoena the root key isn't handed over without our approval. Does Redwood have a mechanism to prevent compelled disclosure?
[00:07:44] Morgan: We provide contractual controls and can restrict access — for BYOK it's governed by your KMS policies; Redwood can't unilaterally unwrap root keys in that model. For hosted without BYOK, we have legal process notes and can work through narrow police/legal requests in line with our policies.
[00:08:01] Elena: Okay. Can you outline the recommended model for us? We're strongly leaning to hosted for operational simplicity, but policy requires that root keys remain under our control.
[00:08:12] Samir: Recommended: Hosted with BYOK + HSM-backed KMS endpoint in your cloud account. That gives you key custody and audit control, while Redwood stores only wrapped key blobs and ephemeral data keys. For ultra low latency you can use Private with an HSM proxy in your VPC.
[00:08:33] Tom: What's involved in the BYOK handshake? API calls, cert exchange?
[00:08:37] Samir: It's a PKI-based mutual TLS handshake. Steps: you provide a public wrapping key (or KMS endpoint + credentials). Redwood generates a data key, requests a wrap operation or wraps with your public wrapping key locally and stores the wrapped blob. There's an optional attestation step to verify the wrapping key is from an approved HSM. We'll send the detailed sequence diagram.
[00:09:01] Elena: A nit — our auditors ask for separation of duties. How do you ensure operators at Redwood can't escalate and access keys?
[00:09:09] Samir: RBAC + break-glass controls. Operators don't have API-level access to the wrapped material; decryption requires service-level operations that are audited. For Private customers we can map your SSO and roles into our RBAC so operations are constrained. For hosted we have strict internal controls, and we can provide SOC 2 evidence.
[00:09:34] Markus: On SSO — can we map our SAML/Okta roles into Redwood so only specific identities can trigger key operations?
[00:09:39] Morgan: Yes. We support SAML/SSO, SCIM provisioning and can sync group membership for RBAC mapping.
[00:09:47] Priya: About key rotation again — do you provide automation hooks for our change control process? E.g., webhooks or events when rotation completes so we can close tickets?
[00:09:56] Samir: Yes, we emit events to the audit stream and have webhooks you can subscribe to. We can also integrate with ticketing via our console or call the API to update a change record.
[00:10:08] Tom: Any known gotchas in multi-region replication and HSM latency?
[00:10:12] Samir: Network latency to remote HSMs is the main one; that's why for cross-region read-heavy workloads we recommend local HSM proxies or caching wrapped data keys with TTLs. Also watch for clock skew when auditing — we recommend NTP sync across systems.
[00:10:29] Elena: Ok that's helpful. Can we talk about test/pilot? We want Redwood to perform a controlled rotation test and show logs to our compliance team.
[00:10:38] Morgan: Absolutely. Proposed pilot: Redwood creates a test tenant in Private lab or in your staging account, we run an automated rotation (data key and root rewrap), show the audit trail, and validate rollback. Samir will run the actual procedures.
[00:10:54] Samir: We'll also measure latency impact on inference and show how caching mitigates that.
[00:10:59] Tom: On the practical side — network ports, firewall rules, and cert exchange — we need a short checklist for our network team.
[00:11:07] Morgan: We'll include a one-page checklist: ports, MTLS cert thumbprint exchange, allowed IP ranges, and sample terraform snippets for Private.
[00:11:16] Elena: For the SOC 2 evidence, can you provide the scope and any redacted reports before our auditor kicks off?
[00:11:22] Jade (CSM): Yes we can provide a redacted SOC 2 Type II and a control mapping that shows where key management and encryption controls live in our matrix. We'll attach that to the playbook.
[00:11:34] Markus: Any contractual clauses we should expect around key custody? E.g., we want an explicit clause that Redwood won't hold keys unless under explicit escrow with multi-sig.
[00:11:42] Morgan: That's standard — we'll surface BYOK and key custody language in the MSA addendum and can work with legal to make it explicit.
[00:11:50] Elena: Alright. I'm seeing an action list — can you recap next steps?
[00:11:55] Morgan: Sure. We'll: 1) send BYOK/HSM playbook and integration diagram, 2) propose pilot schedule and prerequisites, 3) share SOC2 redacted report and log schema. We'll update the ticket with owners and due dates.
[00:12:10] Elena: Great, that's it from our side. Thanks everyone.
[00:12:14] Morgan: Thanks — we'll follow up.
